cues.text: A Boy Who Remembered

Born in the first half of the second century, likely in Smyrna in Asia Minor, Irenaeus tells us himself, in a moving passage of remembrance, that as a boy he had listened to the aged Bishop Polycarp .
A disciple of the Apostle John, he would recount the very words and deeds of the Lord as he had received them from those who had walked with him.
Irenaeus never forgot this.
He carried within him, for the rest of his long life, the conviction that the Church's memory is not an abstraction but a living inheritance.
It was passed hand to hand, voice to voice, from the Apostles themselves down to the humblest believer of his own day.
That conviction would become the very heart of his theology.
A Priest Sent from a Suffering Church
By the 170s Irenaeus was a priest of the Christian community at Lyons in Gaul.
In these very years that Church endured a savage persecution under Marcus Aurelius, in which many of his own flock, including the aged bishop Pothinus, were tortured and put to death for the Faith.
In the midst of this trial, the suffering Christians of Lyons entrusted Irenaeus with a mission to Rome, to carry their counsel to the pope on a delicate controversy troubling the wider Church.
When he returned, it was to find Pothinus already gone to his martyr's crown.
Irenaeus himself was chosen to succeed him as bishop — a pastor set, from the very beginning of his episcopate, in the shadow of the martyrs' witness.
Confronting the Gnostic Illusion
The great struggle of Irenaeus's episcopate was against Gnosticism , a seductive and elaborate system of secret knowledge that claimed to reveal hidden truths beyond the plain Gospel.
It was a maze of invented divine emanations and cosmic dramas.
Irenaeus judged it, with sober and patient clarity, to be a betrayal of the one, simple, saving truth handed down from the Apostles.
His great response, Against Heresies , does not merely refute error but does something more valuable still.
With extraordinary care, it appeals to the apostolic succession preserved in the Churches, giving particular attention to the succession of bishops at Rome.
It shows that the true faith is not a secret possession of the few but the public inheritance of the whole Church, guaranteed by the unbroken chain of apostolic succession.
The Glory of God Is Man Fully Alive
Against the Gnostic contempt for matter and the body, Irenaeus insisted with striking warmth that the flesh, formed by God's own hands, is destined for glory, not escape.
He recognized that contempt as a subtle attack on the goodness of creation itself.
Christ, the New Adam, recapitulated in himself the whole of human history in order to heal and elevate it, not to help us flee from it.

From this conviction comes his most celebrated sentence, one still quoted in every generation: that the glory of God is a human being fully alive , and that the life of a human being consists in beholding God.
Few phrases from the whole of the patristic age speak so directly to us today, in a world so often uncertain of the very dignity of human life that Irenaeus defended.
A Peacemaker Among Churches
Irenaeus's pastoral wisdom extended beyond doctrine to the concord of the whole Church.

When Pope Victor moved to excommunicate the churches of Asia Minor over a dispute about the date of Easter, it was Irenaeus, though himself committed to preserving communion amid differing practices, who wrote urging patience and charity.
He reminded the pope that his own predecessors had tolerated this same diversity of custom without breaking communion.
Unity, for Irenaeus, was never to be purchased at the cost of charity.
Legacy
The date and manner of Irenaeus's death remain uncertain; later, less reliable traditions number him among the martyrs, though the evidence for this is not conclusive.
What is beyond doubt is his legacy.
He stands, in the memory of the Church, as the first great systematic theologian of the apostolic tradition.
He taught every later age to trust that the faith received from the Apostles has been kept whole and entire.
He shows us still, across eighteen centuries, that fidelity to what has been handed down is not a chain upon the mind but the very ground of its freedom.
